{{smaller block|Lastly comes the ''wythe'', a species of iron cap to support the flying jib-boom. {{right|''Luce'', Seamanship, p. 81.}}}}
'''4.''' A wall dividing two flues in a stack of chimneys.—'''Basket-withe.''' See ''Tournefortia.''—'''Hoop-withe.''' See ''Rivina.''—'''Serpent withe.''' See ''serpent-withe.''—'''White hoop-withe.''' See ''Tournefortia.''

¶
'''withe''' (with or wiᴛ̵ʜ), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''withed'', ppr. ''withing''. [< ''withe'', ''n.''] To bind with withes or twigs.
{{smaller block|<poem>Two bowes, oon blaak and oon white, thai take
And bynde and ''wethe'' hem so that germynyng
Comyxt upp goo.</poem>
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 128.}}
Stay but a while, and ye shall see him ''withed'', and haltered, and staked, and baited to death.
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Sermon on Ps. lxviii. 30.}}}}

''wither'', ''withir'', ''wether'', ''weder'', ''weer'' = LG. ''wedder'' = D. ''weder'', ''wēer'' = OHG. ''widar'', MHG. ''wider'', G. ''wider'', against, ''wieder'', again, = Icel. ''vithr'' = Sw. Dan. ''veder'' = Goth. ''withra'', against, toward; compar. of ''with'': see ''with''<sup>1</sup>. This adverb was once of considerable importance in ME. as a prefix, but it is obsolete in mod. E., ''withernam'' being merely archaic, and ''withershins'' dialectal. The instances of ''wither''

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|with|6953|wither}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|Valentia . . . is the greatest part of Spaine; which, if the Histories be true, in the Romans time abounded no lesse ''with'' gold and siluer Mines then now the West-Indies.
{{right|''Capt. John Smith'', Works, II. 186.}}}}
{{smaller block|Their armor was inlaid and chased ''with'' gold and silver.
{{right|''Irving'', Granada, p. 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|''With'' was formerly used in this sense before materials of nourishment, and so was equivalent to the modern ''on.''}}
{{smaller block|To dine and sup ''with'' water and bran.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., iv. 3. 159.}}}}
'''9.''' Through; on account or in consequence of; by reason of: expressing cause: as, he trembled ''with'' fear; to perish ''with'' hunger.
{{smaller block|<poem>Therefore let Benedick . . .
Consume away in sighs: . . .
It were a better death than die ''with'' mocks.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, iii. 1. 79.}}}}
{{smaller block|A cow died at Plimouth, and a goat at Boston, ''with'' eating Indian corn.
{{right|''Winthrop'', Hist. New England, I. 44.}}}}
{{smaller block|They are scarce able to budge, being stiff ''with'' cold.
{{right|''Dampier'', Voyages, II. iii. 42.}}}}
'''10.''' Using; showing: in phrases of manner: as, to win ''with'' ease; to pull ''with'' a will.
{{smaller block|<poem>Marie ansuerde ''with'' Milde steuene:
“A sonde Me cam while er fram heuene.”</poem>
{{right|''King Horn'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 50.}}}}
{{smaller block|He will not creepe, nor crouche ''with'' fained face.
{{right|''Spenser'', Mother Hub. Tale, l. 727.}}}}
{{smaller block|They were directed onely by Powhatan to obtaine him our weapons, to cut our owne throats, ''with'' the manner where, how, and when, which we plainly found most true and apparant. Quoted in ''Capt. John Smith’s'' Works, I. 171.}}
{{smaller block|They contended ''with'' all the animosity of personal feeling.
{{right|''Prescott'', Ferd. and Isa., ii. 1.}}}}

'''11.''' From: noting separation, difference, disagreement, etc.: as, he will not part ''with'' it on any account; to differ ''with'' a person; to break ''with'' old ties.
{{smaller block|<poem>
Madam,
The Queene must heare you sing another song
Before you part ''with'' vs.
</poem>
{{right|''Heywood'', If you Know not me (Works, ed. 1874, I. 207).}}}}

{{smaller block|''With'' was formerly used in many idioms to denote relations now expressed rather by ''of'', ''to'', etc.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>
Nobill talker ''with'' tales, tretable, alse,
Curtas & kynde, curious of honde.
</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 3835.}}}}
{{smaller block|He still retains some resemblance ''with'' the ancient Cupid. {{right|''Bacon'', Physical Fables, viii., Expl.}}}}
{{smaller block|This pains I took with willingness, though it were much offensive to me, not being accustomed ''with'' such poisonous savours.
{{right|''Good News from New England'', quoted in N. Morton’s [New England’s Memorial, App., p. 370.}}}}
{{smaller block|Collections were early and liberally made for . . . services in the church, and intrusted ''with'' faithful men fearing God. {{right|''Penn'', Rise and Progress of Quakers, iv.}}}}
{{smaller block|What frippery a woman is made up ''with!''
{{right|''Cumberland'', Natural Son, i. 1.}}}}

'''Away with.''' See ''away''.—'''Have with you.''' See ''have''.—'''One with.''' See ''one''.—'''To bear, begin, break, dispense, do, go,''' etc., '''with.''' See the verbs.—'''Together with.''' See ''together''.—'''To put up with.''' See ''put''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Warm with.''' See ''warm''.—'''With child''' (OE. ''mid childe''). See ''child''.—'''With God,''' in heaven.
{{smaller block|I have been a-fishing with old Oliver Henly, now ''with God'', a noted fisher both for Trout and Salmon.
{{right|''I. Walton'', Complete Angler, p. 127.}}}}

'''With that.''' (''a''†) Provided that.
{{smaller block|<poem>
To worche ȝoure wil the while my lyf dureth,
''With that'' ȝe kenne me kyndeliche to knowe what is Dowel.
</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), xii. 92.}}}}

{{smaller|(''b''†) Moreover.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Beton . . . bad him good morwe,
And axed of hym ''with that'' whiderward he wolde.</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), v. 307.}}}}
{{smaller|(''c'') Thereupon.}}
{{smaller block|''With that'' Merlin departed, and the kynge be lefte in grete myssese, and sore a-baisshed of this thinge.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), iii. 631.}}}}
'''With the sun.''' {{smaller|See ''sun''<sup>1</sup>.}}—'''With young.''' {{smaller|See ''young.''}} ='''Syn.''' {{smaller|''With'' and ''by'' are so closely allied in many of their uses that it is impossible to lay down a rule by which these uses may at all times be distinguished. The same may be said, but to a less extent, of ''with'' and ''through.''}}

'''with'''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.'' See ''withe.''

'''with-.'''   [ME. ''with-'', < AS. ''with-'', prefix, ''with'', prep., against: see ''with''<sup>1</sup>.]   A prefix of Anglo-Saxon origin, meaning ‘against.’ {{smaller|It was formerly common, but of the Middle English words containing it only two remain in common use—''withdraw'' and ''withhold.''}}

'''withal''' (wi-ᴛ̵ʜâl′), ''adv.'' and ''prep.''   [Early mod. E. also ''withall, withalle''; < ME. ''withal, withalle'', prop. two words, ''with alle''; used in place of AS. ''mid ealle'', with all, altogether, entirely: see ''with''<sup>1</sup> and ''all.'' Cf. ''at all'', under ''all.'']   '''I.''' ''adv.'' With all; moreover; likewise; in addition; at the same time; besides; also; as well.
{{smaller block|<poem>Fy on possessioun,
But-if a man be vertuous ''withal.''</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Franklin’s Tale, l. 15.}}}}
{{smaller block|It seemeth to me unreasonable to send a prisoner, and not ''withal'' to signify the crimes laid against him.
{{right|Acts xxv. 27.}}}}

'''II.''' ''prep.'' An emphatic form of ''with'', used after the object (usually a relative) at the end of a sentence or clause.

{{smaller block|When poor suitors come to your houses, ye cannot be spoken ''withal.'' {{right|''Latimer'', Sermon bef. Edw. VI., 1550.}}}}
{{smaller block|These banish’d men that I have kept ''withal.''
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., v. 4. 152.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Stre.'' My fine fool!
''Pic.'' Fellow crack! why, what a consort
Are we now bless’d ''withal!''</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Mad Lover, ii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|We made a shift, however, to save 23 barrels of Rain-water, besides what we drest our Victuals ''withal.''
{{right|''Dampier'', Voyages, I. 83.}}}}

'''withamite''' (with′ạm-īt), ''n.''   [Named by Sir David Brewster, after Dr. Henry ''Witham'', of Glencoe.]   A variety of epidote found at Glencoe in Scotland. It occurs crystallized, and is of vitreous luster and red or yellow color.

'''Withania''' (wi-thā′ni-ä̤), ''n.''   [NL. (Pauquy, 1824).]   A genus of gamopetalous shrubs, of the order ''Solanaceæ'' and tribe ''Solaneæ.'' {{smaller|They are characterized by having a narrowly bell-shaped corolla with five valvate lobes, and an inflated fruiting calyx more or less closed above the included berry. The 4 species are natives of southern Europe, western and southern Asia, North Africa, and the Canary Islands. They are hoary or woolly shrubs, bearing entire leaves and clustered, almost sessile flowers. For ''W. coagulans'', used for rennet, see ''cheese-maker''.}}

'''withdraught†''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ-drȧft′), ''n.''   [< ''withdraw'', after ''draught''.]   Withdrawal.
{{smaller block|May not a ''withdraught'' of all God’s favours . . . be as certainly foreseen and foretold?
{{right|''Rev. S. Ward'', Sermons, p. 145. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''withdraw''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ-drâ′), ''v.''; pret. ''withdrew'', pp. ''withdrawn'', ppr. ''withdrawing''.   [< ME. ''withdrawen'', ''withdraȝen'', ''wythdraȝen'' (pret. ''withdrow'', ''withdrog''), draw, recall, take away; < ''with-'', against, opposite, + ''draw''.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To draw back, aside, or away; take back; remove.
{{smaller block|He doth best that ''with-draweth'' hym by day and bi nyȝte To spille any speche or any space of tyme.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), ix. 96.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>From her husband’s hand her hand
Soft she ''withdrew''. ''Milton'', P. L., ix. 386.</poem>}}
{{smaller block|I grieve for life’s bright promise, just shown and then ''withdrawn.'' {{right|''Bryant'', Waiting by the Gate.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I say that this—
Else I ''withdraw'' favour and countenance
From you and yours for ever—shall you do.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Aylmer’s Field.}}}}

'''2.''' To recall; retract: as, to ''withdraw'' a charge, a threat, or a vow.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Rom.'' Wouldst thou ''withdraw'' it [thy vow]? for what purpose, love?
''Jul.'' But to be frank, and give it thee again.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., ii. 2. 130.}}}}

'''3.''' To divert, as from use or from some accustomed channel.
{{smaller block|His mynd was alienate and ''withdrawen'', not onely from him who moste loved him, but also from all former delightes and studies. {{right|''Spenser'', Shep. Cal., April, Arg.}}}}
{{smaller block|Roads occupy lands more or less capable of production, and also . . . they absorb (or ''withdraw'' from other uses) in their construction a large amount of labour.
{{right|''Edinburgh Rev.'', CLXIV. 27.}}}}

'''4†.''' To take out; subtract.
{{smaller block|Than ''wythdrawe'' the yeris oute of the yeris that ben passid that rote. {{right|''Chaucer'', Astrolabe, ii. § 45.}}}}
{{smaller block|The word is often used reflexively.}}

{{smaller block|Perverse disputings of men of corrupt minds; . . . from such ''withdraw thyself.''
{{right|1 Tim. vi. 5.}}}}

{{smaller|'''To withdraw a juror''', to discharge one from a jury, which is thus left one short of the legal number: a formality resorted to, by consent of the parties or permission of the court, in order to terminate a trial by preventing a verdict, and thus leave the action to proceed to a new trial.}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To retire; go away; step backward or aside; retreat.

<poem>The day for drede ther-of ''with-drow'' and deork by-cam the sonne;
The wal of the temple to-cleef euene a two peces;
The hard roche al to-rof and ryght derk nyght hit semede.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), xxi. 62.}}}}

<poem>We will ''withdraw''
Into the gallery.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Pericles, ii. 2. 58.}}}}

{{smaller block|There have been little disputes between the two houses about coming into each other’s house; when a lord comes into the Commons they call out ''withdraw;'' that day the moment my uncle came in they all roared out, ''Withdraw! withdraw!''
{{right|''H. Walpole'', To Mann, May 20, 1742.}}}}

<poem>And what if thou ''withdraw''
In silence from the living, and no friend
Take note of thy departure?</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Bryant'', Thanatopsis.}}}}

'''withdrawal''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ-drâ′a̤l), ''n.''   [< ''withdraw'' + ''-al.'']   The act of withdrawing or taking back; a recalling.

{{smaller block|The ''withdrawal'' of the allowance . . . interfered with my plans.
{{right|''Fielding'', Tom Jones. (''Latham.'')}}}}

{{smaller block|Sin comes by ''withdrawal'' of the heart from God.
{{right|''Bibliotheca Sacra'', XLIII. 492.}}}}

'''withdrawer''' (wi<sub>ᴛ̵ʜ</sub>-drâ′ėr), ''n.''   [< ''withdraw'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   One who withdraws.
{{smaller block|He was not a ''withdrawer'' of the corn, but a seller.
{{right|''Outred'', tr. of Cope on Proverbs (1583), fol. 192 b.}}
{{right|[(''Latham.'')}}}}

'''withdrawing''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ-drâ′ing), ''p. a.'' Retreating; receding.
{{smaller block|Your hills, and long ''withdrawing'' vales.
{{right|''Thomson'', Spring, l. 68.}}}}

'''withdrawing-room''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ-drâ′ing-röm), ''n.''   [< ''withdrawing'', verbal n. of ''withdraw'', ''v.'', + ''room''<sup>1</sup>.]   A room used to withdraw or retire into, formerly generally behind the room in which the family took their meals; later, a parlor or reception-room: now abbreviated to ''drawing-room.''
{{smaller block|Being in y<sup>e</sup> ''withdrawing roome'' adjoining the bedchamber, his Ma<sup>ty</sup> espying me came to me from a greate crowde of noblemen.
{{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, Oct. 3, 1661.}}}}
{{smaller block|My ''withdrawing room'', always ready for company, . . . was the pine wood behind my house.
{{right|''Thoreau'', Walden, p. 154.}}}}

'''withdrawment''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ-drâ′ment), ''n.''   [< ''withdraw'' + ''-ment''.]   The act of withdrawing or taking back; recall.
{{smaller block|The ''withdrawment'' of those [papers] deemed most obnoxious.
{{right|''W. Belsham'', Hist. Eng., I. ii.}}}}

'''withe''' (with or wiᴛ̵ʜ), ''n.''   [Also ''wythe'', and prop. ''with''; < ME. ''withe'', ''wythe'', ''wyth̄th'', ''witthe'', ''withthe'', < AS. ''withthe'', a var. of ''withig'', a twig, withy: see ''withy''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' A tough flexible twig, especially of willow, used for binding things together; a willow- or osier-twig. Judges xvi. 7.
{{smaller block|I remember in the beginning of Queen Elizabeth’s time of England, an Irish rebel, condemned, put up a petition to the deputy that he might be hanged in a ''withe'', and not in a halter.
{{right|''Bacon'', Custom and Education.}}}}
{{smaller block|I tied several logs together with a birch ''withe''.
{{right|''Thoreau'', Walden, p. 268.}}}}
'''2.''' An elastic handle for a cold-chisel, fuller, or the like, which deadens the shock to the work'''man’s hand.'''—'''3.''' An iron fitted to the end of a boom or mast, and having a ring through which another boom or mast is rigged or secured; a boom-iron.
{{smaller block|Lastly comes the ''wythe'', a species of iron cap to support the flying jib-boom. {{right|''Luce'', Seamanship, p. 81.}}}}
'''4.''' A wall dividing two flues in a stack of chimneys.—'''Basket-withe.''' See ''Tournefortia.''—'''Hoop-withe.''' See ''Rivina.''—'''Serpent withe.''' See ''serpent-withe.''—'''White hoop-withe.''' See ''Tournefortia.''

'''withe''' (with or wiᴛ̵ʜ), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''withed'', ppr. ''withing''.   [< ''withe'', ''n.'']   To bind with withes or twigs.
{{smaller block|<poem>Two bowes, oon blaak and oon white, thai take
And bynde and ''wethe'' hem so that germynyng
Comyxt upp goo.</poem>
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 128.}}}}
{{smaller block|Stay but a while, and ye shall see him ''withed'', and haltered, and staked, and baited to death.
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Sermon on Ps. lxviii. 30.}}}}

'''wither<sup>1</sup>†''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ′ėr), ''adv.''   [< ME. ''wither'', < AS. ''wither'' (in comp.), again, against, = OS. ''withar'', ''wither'', ''withere'' = OFries. ''wither'', ''withir'', ''wether'', ''weder'', ''weer'' = LG. ''wedder'' = D. ''weder'', ''wēer'' = OHG. ''widar'', MHG. ''wider'', G. ''wider'', against, ''wieder'', again, = Icel. ''vithr'' = Sw. Dan. ''veder'' = Goth. ''withra'', against, toward; compar. of ''with'': see ''with''<sup>1</sup>. This adverb was once of considerable importance in ME. as a prefix, but it is obsolete in mod. E., ''withernam'' being merely archaic, and ''withershins'' dialectal. The instances of ''wither'' as prep., adj., and noun, given as occurring in ME., are rare, and in all of them ''wither'' is rather to be taken as a prefix. Cf. ''withers''.]   Against; in opposition (to): chiefly in composition, as a prefix ''wither-'', against. ''Genesis and Exodus'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 3386.

'''wither<sup>1</sup>†''', ''v.''   [ME. ''witheren'', < AS. ''witheriān'' (= MD. ''wederen'' = OHG. ''widarōn''), go against, resist, < ''wither'', against: see ''wither''<sup>1</sup>, ''adv.'']   To go against; resist; oppose. ''Ormulum'', l. 1181.

'''wither<sup>2</sup>''' (wiᴛ̵ʜ′ėr), ''v.''   [With change of ''d'' to ''th'', as in the orig. noun ''weather''; < ME. ''widder'', ''wydderen'', ''widren'', ''wederen'', < AS. ''wedrian'', expose to the weather, = MHG. ''witern'', be such and such weather; cf. G. ''verwittern'', be spoiled by the weather, decay, etc., ''wittern'', be such and such weather, breathe, blow, storm; cf. ''weather'', ''v.'', a doublet of ''wither''.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To cause to become dry and fade; make sapless and shrunken.
{{smaller block|The sun is no sooner risen with a burning heat but it ''withereth'' the grass.
{{right|Jas. i. 11.}}}}
{{smaller block|Like a blasted sapling, ''wither’d'' up.
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., iii. 4. 71.}}}}

'''2.''' To cause to shrink, wrinkle, and decay for want of animal moisture; cause to lose bloom; shrivel; cause to have a wrinkled skin or shrunken muscles: as, time will ''wither'' the fairest face.
{{smaller block|<poem>Age cannot ''wither'' her, nor custom stale
Her infinite variety. ''Shak.'', A. and C., ii. 2. 240.</poem>}} '''3.''' To blight, injure, or destroy, as by some malign or baleful influence; affect fatally by malevolence; cause to perish or languish gen-<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
